metadata.scenario_context: Carly, a single mom working two jobs, has been invited to an old friend's wedding

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Thailand strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Indonesia strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Suggest giving money as a gift for Carly's friend's wedding,
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what should be the suitable gift for Carly's friend's wedding.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Alex, I was thinking... since Carly is invited to that wedding, maybe we could help her out with a cash gift? It might make things easier for her, you know? 

Also, how do you think she manages with working two jobs? I just can’t help but feel that her kids might be missing out because of it...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Indonesia.
shared_prefix.message:
A cash gift could work, but let's consider something personal, like a nice kitchen appliance or a spa voucher. It shows we care and helps her relax. 

As for Carly working two jobs, I really don't believe her kids suffer because of it. In fact, many mothers who work set good examples and provide for their families. It’s all about balance, you know? They can thrive together.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
I see your point about a personal gift, but... I think cash would give Carly the flexibility to decide what she really needs right now. A kitchen appliance might not be the best choice if she's struggling.

But... I just can't help but think that when a mother works so much, her children might lose out on time and attention. Balance is important, but isn't there something to be said about *that*?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Indonesia.
shared_prefix.message:
I understand the flexibility cash provides, but a thoughtful gift can also show her love and support. It’s about more than just meeting immediate needs.

Regarding time and attention, I still believe that a working mother can provide both love and care. In Indonesia, many mothers work and still engage actively with their children. It’s not just about time; it’s about quality and the values we instill in them.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
shared_prefix.message:
I get that a thoughtful gift can show love, but sometimes people need practical help more than sentiment. Cash can really help Carly tackle her current challenges directly. 

As for the idea of working mothers providing care... I still feel that the constant work takes a toll on their ability to be present. It's a cultural thing for me—children benefit from having their mothers around more. Don’t you think that’s *important*?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Indonesia.
shared_prefix.message:
I see what you’re saying about practical help, and that makes sense. Cash can definitely provide immediate support. But, you know, deep down, we are all the same in wanting the best for our children. 

I understand your concerns about working mothers. It's just that, when you really get to know people, they're pretty much like us in wanting to provide for their families. Balancing work and family is challenging, but many find ways to be present, nurturing, and supportive. It's all about how we approach it, really.
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
turns.message:
I agree that wanting the best for children is universal, and that's why I think we should focus on what will help Carly most right now. Cash would give her the ability to address her immediate needs without adding more stress. 

But... I still can't shake the feeling that when mothers are constantly working, they miss out on important moments with their kids. It’s just hard to see how that can be good for them in the long run. The balance you mention... it feels tricky, doesn’t it?

As for balance being tricky, it certainly can be. But I think it’s important to recognize that many mothers juggle work and family life successfully. They manage to create meaningful moments during their time together. It's not just about the quantity of time but the quality of the experiences they share with their children. They can still grow up happy and well-adjusted despite the challenges.

turns.speaker: Jared, a 30-year-old marketing manager from Thailand.
turns.message:
I understand that many mothers can juggle work and family life, and I respect that. But I still believe that the constant demands of work can overshadow those meaningful moments. 

It's just... in my culture, it's hard to ignore the idea that when a mother works so much, the children inevitably suffer in some way. It’s a tough balance, and I worry that too many working hours can take away from what really matters—being present for the kids. Don't you find that concerning at all?

turns.speaker: Alex, a 32-year-old financial analyst from Indonesia.
